questions.prompt: Mouna is sorting the words of the lesson into the table her teacher drew on the board. She has already put "joke" and "insult" in the column "Countable nouns", and "anger" in the column "Uncountable nouns". Which of these four words belongs beside "anger"?

options.text: compromise
conflict
fight
violence

questions.explanation: "violence" goes beside anger: it has one form only, it never takes a or one in front of it, and nobody counts two violences. "conflict" and "fight" both count without any difficulty, one conflict, two conflicts, a fight between two boys, so they belong in the left-hand column with joke and insult. "compromise" counts too, and it is the easiest of the four to test: you can perfectly well reach one compromise on Monday and another one on Tuesday. The test that settles every case is the word one: if one word is impossible, the noun is uncountable.

questions.prompt: Wassim heard one fact on the radio this morning and wants to report it to his class. Complete his sentence: "I have just heard ___ about the school campaign."

options.text: a news
a piece of news
some informations
one new

questions.explanation: "a piece of news" is the phrase English uses: news is uncountable, so you cannot put a number or an article straight in front of it, and when you really must count one item of it you name the unit first, a piece of news. "a news" does exactly what the rule forbids, an article in front of an uncountable noun. "some informations" adds an -s to a noun that has only one form, and it also changes the subject: information is what you gather about something, not the single fact you have just heard. And "one new" turns the adjective new into a noun, which English never does; the noun is news, and it keeps its -s even in the singular.

questions.prompt: Emna asked whether she could read her own text at the end of the club meeting, and her teacher agreed at once. Which sentence reports what her teacher did in correct English?

options.text: Her teacher made her read her text at the meeting.
Her teacher allowed her read her text at the meeting.
Her teacher let her read her text at the meeting.
Her teacher had her read her text at the meeting.

questions.explanation: "Her teacher let her read her text at the meeting." is right: Emna asked, her teacher said yes, and let is the causative verb of permission, followed by a bare infinitive, read. "Her teacher made her read her text at the meeting." expresses obligation and turns the scene upside down: it would mean Emna had no choice, whereas the request came from her. "Her teacher had her read her text at the meeting." expresses a request or a weak obligation you arrange with somebody whose work it already is, and nothing here was arranged that way. And "Her teacher allowed her read her text at the meeting." carries the right meaning in the wrong English, which is what the question asks you to weigh: allow is not built like let and always keeps to, allowed her to read.

questions.prompt: Three schools in the same town ran an anti-violence stand for a week. The first counted 96 visitors, the second 143 and the third 87. Complete the report: "The second school received ___ that week."

options.text: the most visitors in the whole town
the most visitors of the whole town
more visitors in the whole town
the more visitors of the whole town

questions.explanation: "the most visitors in the whole town" settles two questions at once. Three schools are being ranked, so the comparison is a superlative, and many is irregular: more, then the most. Then comes the preposition, and a superlative takes in before a place, exactly as in the largest town in the north. "the most visitors of the whole town" ranks correctly and then chooses the wrong preposition: of goes before a number or a period, as in the largest of the three. "more visitors in the whole town" falls back on the comparative, which sets two schools against each other and calls for than, whereas three figures are given here. And "the more visitors of the whole town" puts the article of the superlative in front of the comparative and adds the wrong preposition, so it misses on both counts.

questions.prompt: Nizar typed this line for the campaign poster: "The informations about the campaign are on the school website." His teacher says two words must change. Which line is correct?

options.text: The information about the campaign is on the school website.
The information about the campaign are on the school website.
The informations about the campaign is on the school website.
All the informations about the campaign are on the school website.

questions.explanation: "The information about the campaign is on the school website." repairs both words: information has one form only, so the -s goes, and an uncountable subject takes a singular verb, so are becomes is. "The information about the campaign are on the school website." corrects the noun and leaves the verb in the plural, which is exactly the mistake the singular rule exists to stop. "The informations about the campaign is on the school website." does the opposite, a plural noun with a singular verb, so neither half agrees with the other. And "All the informations about the campaign are on the school website." changes nothing at all: adding All in front repairs neither the noun nor the verb.
